items.question: What kind of deployment model do you think will win out for enterprise generative AI in the long term?
items.object: Long-term enterprise generative AI deployment models
items.answer: In the long term, I do think that something in the middle is going to win out. It's a new technology. It's very complicated. And I wish it weren't the case. I wish it were much easier for enterprises to adopt the technology. But sometimes they need help. So some degree of support is just going to be necessary to integrate it into the economy, into all of these different companies, and target all the different applications that they might need to go after.

items.question: Why do you see enterprise AI agents as presenting unusual deployment challenges?
items.object: Enterprise AI agents' access and integration requirements
items.answer:
I also think AI is unique, and these agents are unique, in that an agent can only do its job effectively at driving automation if it has access to the same things the humans have access to. And so that demands a lot of access. It needs to be able to see into your emails, your chat, your calls, your CRM, your ERP, your HR software. It needs so much context. And so that presents a couple different problems. The first is privacy. There's very little software that needs that degree of access. And so privacy is a way bigger issue in AI and agents than it is in other types of enterprise software. So that's something that I think we do uniquely well.

The second piece is each company uses a different tapestry or mosaic of software for their humans, right? There's no standard setup of a company, of what stack they run on. And so each one is different, and each one requires some degree of custom setup to bring all of that context together and integrate it into the model. It's another thing we're spending a lot of time on: making our new agent platform North much easier to customize and integrate with whatever that tapestry might be for each particular company.

items.answer: I mean, definitely, that would be extremely helpful if setup could be completely self-serve and the agents just go off and do what's necessary. items.question: How do you categorize enterprise generative AI use cases that you see as having product-market fit today?
items.object: Enterprise generative AI use cases with product-market fit
items.answer: It's really hard to categorize. I think there's some vertical applications. For example, in healthcare, we really want to make note-taking and form-filling much easier for doctors. Having passive listening mics and being able to listen to that doctor-patient interaction and pre-populate things so that they're not spending half their time typing notes and that type of thing. I think that's very vertical-specific, but much more of what we see are these general categories. Customer support is something where the technology is ready and the need is very much there, and so that's moving quite quickly across verticals—in telco, in healthcare, in financial services. Everybody needs this capability, and the technology is there for it.

items.question: Where do you see the value of AI agents that augment human research?
items.object: AI agents that augment human research
items.answer: I don't know really how to categorize this, but I guess research: augmenting humans with an agent that can go off and do a month's worth of research in an hour or two. We're seeing a lot of demand for that sort of capability. You can imagine if you're in a bank and you have wealth managers, the wealth manager might manage a pool of 20, 50 different clients, and those clients might call that wealth manager up and say, "Hey, I want to hedge against this geopolitical event that might happen in the future." And that wealth manager then needs to go and do research and come up with a strategy: how do I actually even hedge that thing? And it's super time-sensitive because that might be days away, especially in this current moment. It's very relevant right now. But if we can make that dramatically more effective because these models can read hundreds of thousands of times as much as a human and come back with a very robust piece of research with citations back to all the source documents so the human can audit it, I think we can just make knowledge work 10x more effective and productive.

items.question: Why do you see reasoning as an essential capability for language models?
items.object: Reasoning models and variable effort
items.answer: Reasoning is so obvious. It's insane that anyone would be content with non-reasoning models, because what is the input space? It's language. It's everything. It's everything from, "Hey, what's one plus one?" chatbot to, you know, prove Fermat's last theorem. And so the input space is everything, and we shouldn't expect the model to spend the same amount of time to answer those two questions. The fact that reasoning unlocks a capability for the technology to spend different amounts of energy on different complexities of problem is so obvious and intuitive. We know we have to have that capability built into the technology.

items.question: What do you think today's language models are missing in their ability to learn from experience?
items.object: Language models learning from experience
items.answer: There's more that's missing, for sure. For instance, the status quo with models: we spend all this money training them. We spend $100 million building a model, and then we get our final checkpoint, final weights, and we just distribute that to the world and they're frozen, and everyone is speaking to the same version of the model. It doesn't remember your chats from months ago. And so there's no notion of learning from experience. That's a clear capability that humans have, right? We can start dumb at something new and then become an expert over the course of four or five years of practicing that. These models should have the exact same ability to learn from their experience out in the world and learn from feedback from the humans that they interact with. So there are these obvious properties of intelligence that are missing in the technology and that will need to come.

items.question: How do you view the emerging limits of the “scale is all you need” approach to AI development?
items.object: The “scale is all you need” hypothesis
items.answer: But I do think there's a change that's happening right now, which is the whole "scale is all you need" hypothesis is breaking. We're very heavy into diminishing returns of capital and compute. We're going to have to become smarter and more creative in order to unlock the next step up in the technology. But I think that's good. It's good pressure on us as innovators to go out and explore and try things out. The old strategy was boring and dumb. So I'm excited for the new era.

items.question: How do you now think about the need for specialized AI models within an organization?
items.object: Specialized AI models versus general models within organizations
items.answer:
I used to think much more that we needed specialized models. With these models, they're kind of able to self-develop experts, and these are just subnetworks within the model. And so that's alleviated some of the pressure. I would say custom models are still important. There's still fundamental context about a particular business or a particular domain that are missing from models that are built off of the web, which contains a lot of information about humanity, history, culture, science, but there's stuff that is not on the web, and these models need to be able to get good at that to provide value in the world.

I think that's where custom models make a lot of sense, closing that gap. There's not a lot of manufacturing data out on the web, or customer transactions, or detailed personal health records. For these sorts of modalities or types of data, what Cohere does is partner with the organizations that do have this data to create a custom model that only they have access to, that gets very, very good at working in those domains. But the general models are extraordinary, and synthetic data is able to close the gap considerably. I think certainly there won't be tens or hundreds of models operating within an organization. You might have a handful, but I don't see it being like every single team is going to have their own fine-tuned model.

items.question: Why do you see a hard dependency on humans in evaluating AI models?
items.object: Human involvement in AI model evaluation
items.answer: Well, I guess definitionally, if you're building models for people, they're probably best seated to evaluate their usefulness. Eval is where you just can't take a human out of the loop. Yet, I mean, the way to get the human out of the loop is to have an expert that is better than your current model observing it. But that assumes you can build that expert in the first place. So there's, I think, a hard dependency on humans within eval.

items.question: How do you think human expertise can be scaled into training data for specialized AI domains like medicine?
items.object: Human expertise and synthetic data for training models in specialized domains
items.answer: On the data-gen side, it's too expensive. We definitely still need human data, but it's too expensive to go find 100,000 doctors and have them teach the model to do medicine. That is not a viable strategy. It was a viable strategy to teach the model general things about how to converse, chitchat, that type of thing, to find 100,000 average people and they can teach the model to do that stuff. So we've had to become much more creative. Teaching the model to chitchat and do all that stuff unlocked a certain degree of freedom in terms of synthetic data generation, which we can then apply to these specific domains like medicine. We can use a much smaller pool of human data. Maybe I go to 100 doctors and get them to provide me some lessons and teach my model. Then I use that pool of known-good, very trustworthy data to generate a thousandfold synthetic lookalike data. In verifiable domains like code and math it's way easier because you can check the results and use that to filter the synthetic data and pull out the garbage and find the gold. In other domains it becomes much more complex, but it's still viable. At this stage, in terms of the overall data that Cohere is generating for a new model, an overwhelming majority is synthetic.

items.question: How do you see the value of test-time compute for reasoning in enterprise AI?
items.object: Test-time compute and reasoning for enterprise tasks
items.answer:
Cohere cares way less about solving Math Olympiad. We don't have enterprises coming to us begging for models that can do well in Math Olympiad. But we do have them begging us to help them automate processes within the back office that use this piece of software and also go out on the web and do some research and then do this. For us, it's very much about teaching these models to reason through solving the problems that exist within business using the tools that humans in businesses use to get them done today. That's what we care about, and it has been a complete step change in terms of improvement.

There were tasks pre-reasoning we just couldn't get a model accurate enough to accomplish. It was impossible. Models could not solve the problem. They almost always fail. And with reasoning they almost never fail. Pretty much everything you throw at the thing, it'll figure out a way to actually accomplish it. Reasoning's ability to unlock reflection and understanding why the first attempt failed, and then using that to find another path, an alternative path to the same outcome, has been a real unlock.

items.question: What do you find rewarding about watching reasoning models work through complex tasks?
items.object: Reasoning models’ problem-solving traces
items.answer: Yeah, things that just don't work start working. And complex tasks. There's many delightful moments where you're like, "How did it know to look there?" And it's, "Oh, it's because it failed looking in the obvious places." And then you read the reasoning traces, you're like, "Ah, it's actually pretty smart." The reasoning traces are jaw-dropping. It's so beautiful that these models organically problem-solve and think through stuff. They have their own little epiphanies and they're like, "Oh, you know what? I should check over here, and maybe this happened, and that's why it's not over there." That has been super rewarding to see, I guess.

items.question: Why did you decide to push into the application layer with North?
items.object: North and Cohere's move into enterprise applications
items.answer:
With North pushing into the application layer, that was totally motivated by—we were selling models and we just kept seeing our customers building the same thing again and again and again. It would take them like a year to build an application that took models, presented a UI, integrated with all the different tools and data sources, did the privacy and ACL inheritance stuff well. And then it was usually built by the AI team inside these enterprises. They're not product teams, so it's actually not that nice of a user experience, and the people within the company wouldn't want to use it.

So we said, what if we just solve that entire problem for the enterprise? We're going to create a truly consumer-grade product experience that people love to use, is super intuitive, extremely low latency, but ships with all the features that an enterprise needs, like the ability to customize it completely. You can customize the UI, rebrand it however you want. You can customize the data connections and the sources that your model's able to pull from and the tools that it's able to use. You can even, if you want to, let's say you've trained some Llama fine-tune or something on your data, plug Llama in there and expose it through this application. And so it's really just setting a company forward 12 to 18 months in its product roadmap, and they immediately can distribute this tech into the hands of their employees.

items.question: Why do you see Cohere's integration of model development and applications as crucial to product quality?
items.object: Cohere's vertical integration of model development and applications
items.answer: I think we have far more levers to pull to deliver the experience that the customer needs. Because we're vertically integrated, the next version of Command, our generative model, is going to be optimized. Actually, the latest version already is optimized for the use cases that we know our customers need in North. So it knows how to use an ERP. It knows how to build with a CRM. And so that integration between the technology, the models, and what the actual customer needs is something that I think is crucial to product quality. It's part of the reason why a lot of the existing applications are, in my opinion, missing or not fulfilling the product promise that they're making to their users. They're a consumer of the technology. They can grab some Llama weights or something, but they're not able to change that technology for the needs of their customer. And so that presents a fundamental barrier to product quality.

I have passports in both of those places, also in Canada. The leadership team is from all over. We try to be a partner to these countries in adopting the technology and making sure that it works for them.

items.question: Why do you consider the multilingual work behind Cohere’s open-source Aya project worth investing in heavily?

items.answer: A lot of our work on the open-source side with Cohere, the Aya project, was the largest data collection effort for any machine learning project. items.question: How do you think the research culture you experienced at Google Brain should translate to Cohere's pursuit of an AI product?
items.object: Google Brain's research culture and Cohere's product-focused research
items.answer:
What was so incredible was it was a home for really brilliant people to do their best work. You got pretty much complete research freedom to do whatever you wanted to do, tons of compute, tons of software infrastructure to use that compute, and really great people to do it with. I think that setup led to some really interesting things.

But it's not the setup that delivers an incredible product. For Cohere the needs are different. We have a very targeted focus: there is something to accomplish. We have an objective, which is driving this automation, making this technology good at using all of this different software. And so the problem set is quite focused. You can't work on whatever you want. There isn't time for that. We have to be much more focused and targeted in terms of where we invest.

What we preserve are incredible people, tons of compute, and the same sort of world-changing ambition that I felt back at Google. And also a warm culture, I think. Maybe things have changed in different labs, but when I was there it was a deeply warm and meaningful, welcoming place to be that cared about something. That's something that we preserve quite well.

items.question: Why do you see AI models learning from experience with users as such an important capability?
items.object: AI models learning from experience with users
items.answer:
Learning from experience. Once models can learn from interacting with the user, just from a what-you-can-build perspective, that capability unlocks so much. Right now with a model that doesn't do that, I give feedback, but when I start a new chat, it's forgotten all that feedback. It's just wasted time. If it can't do something, I'm just annoyed, and then I close the window and go do it myself.

But if a model is kind of like an intern where, hey, it's the first time it's doing this thing. It's going to mess up a little bit. I'll teach it. I'll guide it. I'll give it some feedback. And then, hey, look, you did it, and it never makes those mistakes again. How does that happen, everybody?

I think it probably looks like putting it in a database that can be queried and looked up, and there's just always a context of the previous history of interactions available to the model when it's generating. Probably looks something like that.

But, yeah, you think about what that unlocks: I'm so much more invested in interacting with this model because it's learning from me. It's growing with me. It starts to know me, know my preferences, know how to do the things that I need it to do because I've spent so much time teaching this thing and I've turned it from my little intern to me 2.0. That connection with the system is something I'm very excited for.

items.question: Why do you think AI will augment people rather than cause mass unemployment?
items.object: AI's effect on employment and economic supply
items.answer: I hope that we're able to drive costs down and that supply increases in the world, because I think we are supply-constrained. We're not demand-constrained, which is why I don't think there's going to be any sort of mass unemployment. I really don't believe in that. So long as we're able to move people onto the spaces that we need them and we can retrain folks, humanity has infinite demand. And so we are fully supply-side constrained. This technology isn't going to displace people. It's going to augment them and let them do more and deliver more of what the world is wanting and needing.

items.question: How has the prospect of faster AI advancement changed the way you live or think about the future?
items.object: Living with the prospect of rapid AI advancement
items.answer: Not remotely. Not at all. Not at all. I'm super excited. I'm super excited. My dad is a cancer survivor. I really hope he lives for a lot longer and that treatments continue to get dramatically better. So I'm really excited about the future, but I don't think it's a utopia. I think it's a much better world, but it's not a utopia. It's not like you should be liquidating all your assets and just going on vacation permanently or something like that. It's just going to be a way better world.

items.question: How do you think the public and policymakers should prioritize the risks posed by AI?
items.object: AI risks and public policy priorities
items.answer:
I worry about them. I worry what sort of capabilities bad actors will be able to access, especially at the state level. I want to make sure that liberal democracies are the first ones to get it and that they establish an advantage. I worry about whether we have the infrastructure in place to facilitate moving people to new careers if particular jobs are impacted. I want to make sure that we have that capacity to move them and retrain them and put people on new, more fulfilling work.

But I'm not afraid of the X-risk, like Terminator takes it, breaks out of the box and gets all of our nukes, or nefariously manipulating people to do what it wants. I really think there's so much to worry about with this technology that the doomsday scenarios aren't where we should have the public and policymakers focus right now. There's more than enough we've got to get right in the near and midterm.
